identity.title: Emergency Action Plan — Portland Facility
identity.issuer: Cascade Specialty Chemicals, LLC (self-authored internal safety document)

scan.summary: This is Cascade's own written Emergency Action Plan for the Portland facility, covering fire, chemical release, medical emergency and earthquake response for its 42 employees. It is a program document the company wrote itself to satisfy Oregon OSHA's emergency-action-plan rule, so what matters is whether its content matches the rule's required elements and whether it is kept current, not an agency approval.
scan.freshness_note: The plan is dated 'Revised February 2021,' more than five years old as of September 2026. Section 6 states the facilities lead reviews the plan every January, but the document itself shows no revision markings since 2021, so either the annual reviews have not produced updates or the document on file is stale. Ask for the most current revised copy.

gaps.title: No procedure for employees who must shut down critical equipment before evacuating
gaps.description: The plan states that on the evacuation alarm 'all employees stop work, secure nothing that requires more than a few seconds, and leave' — but Oregon OSHA's emergency action plan rule requires the plan to address procedures for operating or shutting down critical equipment before evacuation. The document never says whether Cascade has any equipment (pumps, reactive-chemical handling, forklifts, process lines) that needs a controlled shutdown, or names anyone responsible for it.
gaps.fix: Add a subsection that either (a) identifies any equipment or process at the Portland site that requires shutdown before evacuation and names the employee(s) responsible and the steps, or (b) states explicitly that no equipment at the site requires shutdown and all areas can be left running safely.
gaps.locator: not in the document — would belong in Section 3 (Evacuation procedures)
gaps.quote: all employees stop work, secure nothing that requires more than a few seconds, and leave by the nearest marked exit

gaps.title: No stated procedure for how an employee reports a fire or emergency
gaps.description: Section 2 describes the alarm system and pull stations but never tells an employee what to do upon discovering a fire, spill or other emergency — e.g., pull the nearest station, call a specific number, or notify a named person — before the alarm itself sounds.
gaps.fix: Add a short instruction such as: 'Any employee who discovers a fire or hazardous condition immediately activates the nearest pull station and/or calls [number] to notify [role].'
gaps.locator: not in the document — would belong in Section 2 (Alarm system)
gaps.quote: Manual pull stations are located at each exit door.

gaps.title: No named contact for questions about the plan or duties
gaps.description: The rule requires the plan to list the name or job title of an employee who can be contacted for more information about the plan or an explanation of duties under it. The document names roles for emergency response (floor warden, incident coordinator, facilities lead) but never designates one of these, or anyone else, as the point of contact for general questions about the plan itself.
gaps.fix: Add a line naming a job title (e.g., 'Facilities Lead') as the contact for questions about the plan or an employee's duties under it.
gaps.locator: not in the document — would fit in Section 1 (Purpose and scope) or Section 6

facts.affects: Confirms the site is well above the 10-employee threshold under Oregon OSHA / 29 CFR 1910.38(b), so a written (not oral) plan is required — which this document satisfies in form.

facts.quote: The alarm is tested on the first Monday of each month by the facilities lead.
facts.affects: Shows a recurring alarm-system testing schedule, evidence toward the 1910.165/OAR alarm maintenance requirement.

facts.value: twice a year, spring and autumn
facts.quote: Evacuation drills are held twice a year, in spring and autumn.
facts.affects: Establishes the company's own drill cadence; relevant evidence if an inspector asks how the plan is exercised.

facts.quote: The facilities lead reviews the plan every January and updates the evacuation maps whenever the building layout changes.
facts.affects: Sets an expectation of annual review; the document's own 2021 revision date without visible later updates conflicts with this stated cadence.

expected_missing.title: Fire Prevention Plan
expected_missing.why: Oregon OSHA (OAR 437-002-0043) typically pairs a Fire Prevention Plan with an Emergency Action Plan, covering fire hazards, ignition sources and housekeeping — not referenced anywhere in this document.
expected_missing.basis: similar companies, not a checked requirement

expected_missing.title: Hazardous Materials / Chemical Business Emergency Response Plan
expected_missing.why: A chemical distributor handling stored hazardous materials commonly holds a facility hazmat response or business emergency plan (often tied to local fire code or DEQ reporting) beyond the employee evacuation-focused EAP.
expected_missing.basis: similar companies, not a checked requirement

expected_missing.title: Training and drill records
expected_missing.why: The plan references twice-yearly drills and annual warden training, but no log or record of dates, attendance or outcomes is attached — usually kept as a companion record.
expected_missing.basis: similar companies, not a checked requirement

expected_missing.title: Hazard Communication Program / SDS binder location policy
expected_missing.why: The plan mentions bringing 'the SDS for the product' to responders, implying an SDS system exists, but the written Hazard Communication program itself is not part of this document.
expected_missing.basis: similar companies, not a checked requirement

scan.confidence_notes: I am confident in the six required elements of an Oregon OSHA / 29 CFR 1910.38-style emergency action plan and matched them against the document's six sections fairly directly — evacuation, accounting for employees, and rescue/medical duties are clearly and adequately covered. The three gaps flagged (critical-operations shutdown, explicit reporting method, named plan contact) are well-established required elements that I could not find addressed anywhere in the text. I am less certain whether Cascade's Portland site actually has equipment needing a controlled shutdown — if it is a pure distribution/warehouse operation with no continuous process, that gap may be satisfied by simply stating 'not applicable,' which I could not confirm from the document alone.

CASCADE SPECIALTY CHEMICALS, LLC
EMERGENCY ACTION PLAN
Portland Facility, 4410 NW Front Avenue, Portland, Oregon 97210
Revised February 2021
1. Purpose and scope
This Emergency Action Plan describes what employees of Cascade Specialty Chemicals do when there is
a fire, chemical release, medical emergency, earthquake or other emergency at the Portland facility. It
applies to all 42 employees at the Portland facility, including warehouse, drivers, laboratory and office
staff, and to contractors and visitors while on site. The plan is kept in the front office and in the warehouse
break room, and a copy is available to any employee on request.
2. Alarm system
The building has a monitored fire alarm system with audible horns and strobe lights in the warehouse,
laboratory, loading dock and offices. The alarm is monitored 24 hours a day by Cascade Fire & Safety
under a service contract. Manual pull stations are located at each exit door. The alarm is tested on the first
Monday of each month by the facilities lead. A continuous horn means evacuate. Three short horns
repeated means shelter in place because of an outdoor hazard.
3. Evacuation procedures
When the continuous alarm sounds, all employees stop work, secure nothing that requires more than a
few seconds, and leave by the nearest marked exit. Exit routes are posted on the evacuation maps at each
exit door and in Appendix A. Warehouse staff leave by the east dock doors or the north pedestrian door.
Laboratory staff leave by the laboratory's own exterior door on the south wall. Office staff leave by the
main entrance or the west stairwell. Do not use the freight lift. Do not return for belongings.
The assembly point is the far north end of the visitor parking lot, beside the flagpole, at least 150 feet
from the building. Employees assigned as floor wardens (one per area, listed on the warden roster posted
beside each evacuation map) sweep their area, close doors behind them, and report to the assembly point.
For a chemical release outdoors or a hazard that makes leaving the building unsafe, the shelter-in-place
signal sounds. Employees move to the interior conference room or the laboratory corridor, close doors,
and the facilities lead shuts down the building ventilation from the mechanical room panel.
4. Accounting for employees after evacuation
At the assembly point each floor warden takes a headcount of the people from their area against the daily
sign-in sheet and the visitor log, which the receptionist brings out. Any person unaccounted for is reported
at once to the incident coordinator at the assembly point, who passes the information to the fire
department on arrival. No one re-enters the building until the fire department or the incident coordinator
gives the all-clear. Evacuation drills are held twice a year, in spring and autumn.
5. Rescue and medical duties
Employees do not attempt rescue inside the building. First aid is given at the assembly point by the
trained first-aid responders (two per shift, named on the warden roster), who bring the first-aid kit and the
AED from the front office. An employee exposed to a chemical is taken to the emergency shower and
eyewash at the loading dock if it can be reached safely, or to the assembly point, and the SDS for the
product is brought to the responders. Emergency medical services are called for any injury beyond minor
first aid.
6. Training and review
Every new employee is walked through this plan, the exit routes for their work area and the assembly
point on their first day. Floor wardens and first-aid responders are trained annually. The plan is reviewed
with all employees whenever it is changed and whenever an employee's responsibilities under it change.
The facilities lead reviews the plan every January and updates the evacuation maps whenever the building
layout changes.
Appendix A: Evacuation maps (warehouse, laboratory, offices)
Appendix B: Floor warden and first-aid responder roster (posted beside each evacuation map)
